This paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models built on top of foundation-model embeddings. The central claim is that CBMs, despite their interpretability appeal, are not inherently robust under deployment-time distribution shifts, and therefore require adaptation just as standard feature-based predictors do. To address this, the paper proposes CONDA, a three-stage source-free adaptation framework that updates the concept bank, the concept-to-label linear layer, and an added residual concept branch using only unlabeled target data and pseudo-labels derived from the foundation model. The paper also presents a taxonomy of failure modes for CBMs under low-level and concept-level shifts, and evaluates the method across several datasets and several CBM construction approaches.

Overall, I find the paper timely and interesting. The combination of foundation models, concept bottlenecks, and test-time adaptation is novel and relevant, and the empirical results suggest that adaptation can substantially improve deployed CBMs, especially under concept-level shifts where static concept bottlenecks can fail badly. The paper is also commendably broad in evaluating multiple CBM constructions rather than tailoring the method to a single concept-learning pipeline. At the same time, I have significant reservations about the conceptual framing, some methodological choices, and the strength of the evidence supporting the interpretability claims. My assessment is positive but not unreserved: the paper has a strong idea and promising empirical evidence, but several claims should be sharpened and some parts need stronger validation.

The main strength of the paper is its problem formulation. The observation that CBMs can match source-domain performance yet degrade sharply under shift is important and, in my view, underexplored. The paper correctly identifies that interpretability does not imply robustness, and Figure 1 plus the main benchmark table support that point well. The proposed decomposition into concept-score alignment, label-layer adaptation, and residual concept expansion is intuitive and practically appealing. I also appreciate that the method is source-free and does not require retraining the backbone FM, which makes the setting realistic for deployment.

A second strength is the empirical breadth. The experiments cover low-level corruptions, spurious-correlation shifts, and a natural medical shift, and compare against three distinct CBM construction methods. This is much stronger than evaluating only one concept bottleneck variant. The results on Waterbirds and Metashift are particularly compelling for the post-hoc and label-free CBMs: the gains are large, and the adapted CBMs recover much of the gap to feature-based baselines. The component analysis is also useful and broadly consistent with the paper’s intuition that different parts of the CBM should be adapted for different shift types.

That said, the paper’s theoretical framing is weaker than it first appears. The definitions of low-level shift and concept-level shift are not really definitions of shift classes in the usual statistical sense, but rather idealized properties relative to a chosen concept map and classifier. For example, “low-level shift” is defined by invariance of the concept-score distribution, and “concept-level shift” by change in concept-score distribution but invariance of prediction distribution. These are not observable properties of the environment; they depend on the specific concept representation and predictor. As a result, the taxonomy is somewhat circular: a “failure mode” is often just the negation of the assumed invariance property. This does not invalidate the method, but it weakens the formal contribution. I would encourage the authors to present this more modestly as an analytical lens rather than a formal categorization of real-world shifts.

Relatedly, Definition 1 on concept completeness is too strong and somewhat disconnected from the actual method. It requires existence of a classifier over concepts that preserves prediction distributions across source and target for both low-level and concept-level shifts. But the method never tests or estimates completeness in this sense, and the residual branch is introduced as a practical patch for incompleteness rather than a principled estimator of missing concepts. The paper would be stronger if it either developed a tighter connection between this definition and the residual branch, or removed the impression that the theory meaningfully justifies the algorithm.

I also have concerns about the CSA objective. The method assumes access to class-conditional Gaussian statistics of source-domain concept scores, even though the source data are unavailable. This is reasonable if these statistics are stored at training time, but it should be made explicit that this is additional source-side state beyond the CBM parameters. More importantly, the Gaussian assumption seems quite strong for concept scores, especially for heterogeneous concept banks and high-dimensional concept spaces. The paper does not provide evidence that this approximation is adequate, nor compare against simpler alternatives such as matching first and second moments without a Gaussian likelihood interpretation, or using class prototypes only. Since CSA is one of the paper’s core novelties, some validation of this modeling choice would be valuable.

The pseudo-labeling strategy is another important limitation. CONDA relies heavily on pseudo-labels from an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probe FM predictions, and the paper itself acknowledges that performance can collapse when these pseudo-labels are poor. In fact, several negative results already appear in the appendix and even in the main table, where adaptation hurts strong unadapted CBMs. This raises a key question: when should one adapt at all? In practice, a deployment method needs some safeguard against harmful adaptation. The paper currently lacks a confidence-based gating mechanism, early stopping criterion, or adaptation trigger. Without such a mechanism, the method seems risky in exactly the settings where robustness matters most. I view this as one of the most important missing pieces.

The empirical evaluation, while broad, also leaves some gaps. First, the comparisons are mostly against unadapted CBMs and non-interpretable ZS/LP baselines. Since the paper is about test-time adaptation, I would expect stronger baselines from the TTA literature adapted to the same FM+head setting. For example, how does adapting a standard linear probe on FM features with Tent, MEMO, CAFA, or a source-free linear-head adaptation baseline compare to adapting the CBM? Even if those methods are not directly concept-aware, they are the natural competitors in the deployment setting. The current results show that CONDA improves CBMs, but not whether it is the best way to spend the adaptation budget if one cares about accuracy under source-free shift.

Second, the evaluation of interpretability is suggestive but not yet rigorous. The paper argues that adapted concepts are “better aligned with the test data” and presents qualitative examples where concept weights shift in intuitive ways, and residual concepts receive plausible automatic captions such as feathers, wings, and beak. This is interesting, but the evidence is mostly anecdotal and depends on an automatic annotation pipeline that itself uses CLIP-based similarity and a threshold. There is no human evaluation, no quantitative concept quality metric beyond the appendix similarity score, and no test of whether the adapted concepts remain stable, non-redundant, or actionable. Since the method explicitly changes the concept bank at test time, preserving interpretability is a central concern, not a side issue. I think the paper should be more cautious in claiming interpretability gains unless it can support them more directly.

A related concern is that the residual branch may undermine the very bottleneck semantics the paper aims to preserve. Algebraically, the final predictor is just a larger linear map over FM features factored into concept vectors and weights. If the residual concepts are learned from unlabeled target data with a discriminative objective, they may become highly task-useful but only weakly human-meaningful. The paper partially acknowledges an accuracy-interpretability tradeoff in the appendix, which I appreciated. But this tradeoff deserves more prominence in the main paper. In some sense, the method may be moving from “interpretable CBM” toward “sparsely structured linear adaptation with some concept-like directions.” That may still be useful, but it should be framed honestly.

There are also some issues in the experimental setup that deserve clarification. The CIFAR-C experiments use corruption severity 2 rather than the more standard severity 5, justified by the need for the FM to remain a decent pseudo-label oracle. This is understandable, but it also means the low-level shift setting is somewhat selected to favor the method. The appendix does include a harsher negative case, which is good, but the main paper should more clearly state that the method depends on a reasonably robust FM oracle. Similarly, the use of adversarially fine-tuned FARE2 CLIP on CIFAR may make the pseudo-labeling unusually strong relative to standard CLIP. This is not unfair, but it complicates the claim that the method broadly applies to arbitrary foundation models.

I also found some presentation issues. Equation numbering appears inconsistent in a few places, and there are minor typographical problems. More substantively, the notation-heavy formalism in Section 2 may give an impression of rigor without yielding concrete guarantees. The paper might actually improve if that section were simplified and the saved space used for stronger empirical analysis, especially around adaptation failure detection and interpretability validation.

Despite these criticisms, I think the paper makes a meaningful contribution. The idea that concept bottlenecks should be adapted post-deployment, and that different parts of the CBM fail under different shifts, is valuable. The method is sensible and appears effective in several important settings. The work also opens a useful research direction at the intersection of interpretability and adaptation, where there is currently little prior art.

For improvement, I would most strongly recommend the following. First, add stronger adaptation baselines from the TTA/source-free adaptation literature, especially on FM features and linear heads, to contextualize the gains. Second, include an adaptation safety mechanism or at least an analysis of when adaptation should be skipped, perhaps based on pseudo-label confidence, agreement between ZS and LP, or validation-free risk proxies. Third, strengthen the interpretability evaluation with either human judgments, concept purity/coherence metrics, intervention-style analyses, or stability analyses across runs and batches. Fourth, better justify or ablate the CSA Gaussian assumption and the need for source-side class-conditional covariance storage. Fifth, tone down the formal claims in Section 2 or connect them more tightly to the algorithm.

My overall recommendation is moderately positive. I see clear novelty and practical relevance, and the empirical results are promising, especially for concept-level shifts. However, the paper would be substantially stronger with more rigorous baselines and a more careful treatment of interpretability and adaptation risk. If accepted, I would encourage the authors to revise the framing and strengthen the empirical support for the broader claims.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models (CBMs) built on top of foundation model embeddings under distribution shift. It identifies three failure modes for deployed CBMs—non-robust concept bottlenecks under low-level shifts, non-robust concept-to-label classifiers under concept-level shifts, and incomplete concept sets—and proposes CONDA, a three-stage source-free adaptation framework using only unlabeled target data. CONDA performs concept-score alignment (CSA) by adapting concept vectors toward source class-conditional Gaussian statistics, linear probing adaptation (LPA) by updating the concept-to-label layer with pseudo-labels, and a residual concept bottleneck (RCB) that adds new concepts to compensate for incompleteness. Experiments across CIFAR10/100-C, Waterbirds, MetaShift, and Camelyon17 with several CBM constructions show substantial gains over unadapted CBMs in many settings, especially for post-hoc and label-free CBMs, and qualitative analyses suggest adapted concepts better reflect target-domain correlations.
strengths: Addresses an interesting and underexplored problem: test-time adaptation for interpretable concept bottleneck pipelines built on foundation models.
The decomposition into three failure modes is intuitive and helps motivate the modular design of CSA, LPA, and RCB.
Method is practically appealing in the source-free unlabeled target setting and is compatible with multiple CBM construction methods and multiple FM backbones.
Empirical evaluation spans several datasets, shift types, and CBM variants, and shows large improvements over unadapted CBMs in many cases, especially on Waterbirds and MetaShift.
Ablations on individual components and pseudo-labeling variants provide useful evidence that different modules matter under different shift types.
The paper is generally well organized and includes runtime discussion and qualitative interpretability analyses of adapted/residual concepts.
weaknesses: The theoretical formalization of shift types and completeness is largely definitional and not tied to guarantees for the proposed algorithm; the paper does not establish when CSA/LPA/RCB should succeed or fail.

The central adaptation mechanism depends heavily on pseudo-label quality from zero-shot/linear-probe FM predictions, making gains partly attributable to the robustness of the non-interpretable teacher rather than the CBM adaptation itself.

Several empirical claims are overstated relative to the results: adaptation does not consistently match or exceed non-interpretable baselines across datasets/CBM types, and sometimes degrades performance substantially.

Comparisons against standard test-time adaptation baselines adapted to the same FM features or classifier family are limited; the paper mainly compares against unadapted CBMs rather than strong source-free/TTA methods on the same downstream predictor.
Interpretability claims are mostly qualitative and not rigorously quantified; adding residual concepts increases capacity and may weaken the bottleneck semantics.
The method introduces many hyperparameters and stage-specific design choices, with limited evidence of robustness across settings beyond selected ablations.
methodological_flaws: The shift taxonomy is scientifically weak as stated: defining low-level shift by equality of concept-score distributions and concept-level shift by equality of prediction distributions makes the categories model-dependent and partly tautological. Real shifts are not known a priori to satisfy these equalities, so the formalization does not support the later claims strongly.

Definition 1 of concept completeness is problematic: it is phrased in terms of equality of prediction distributions across domains rather than correctness or conditional sufficiency for labels. Matching prediction distributions is neither necessary nor sufficient for robust classification, so the notion of completeness is not well aligned with the CBM literature.

CSA assumes class-conditional Gaussian distributions of source concept scores and access to their means/covariances, but there is no validation that this approximation is reasonable for the tested CBMs. The Mahalanobis-based objective is therefore heuristic, and no sensitivity to covariance estimation, singularity, or class imbalance is analyzed.

The Mahalanobis distance formula appears to contain a typographical/mathematical error in the text: the final factor is written as (v_C(x_t)) - mu_y) rather than (v_C(x_t)-mu_y), suggesting insufficient care in the mathematical presentation.

The CSA objective minimizes log(D_intra/D_inter) using pseudo-labels from external predictors. If pseudo-labels are wrong, CSA can explicitly pull concept vectors toward incorrect class statistics. This failure mode is acknowledged but not adequately controlled, and no confidence-thresholding or uncertainty-aware weighting is built into the main method.

The empirical protocol may bias results in favor of the method by choosing CIFAR-C severity level 2 because higher severities make pseudo-labeling unreliable. While understandable, this weakens claims about robustness under distribution shift and suggests the method is effective only when the FM teacher is already fairly robust.

The online adaptation protocol predicts on the same batch used for adaptation, which can inflate apparent performance relative to a strictly prequential evaluation where each sample is predicted before being used for adaptation. The paper does not clearly justify this choice or compare against stricter online evaluation.

The residual branch effectively adds a linear residual classifier in feature space via W~C~, increasing model capacity. Improvements may therefore stem from added expressive power rather than concept completion per se. There is no control baseline with an equally sized non-concept residual linear adapter to isolate the benefit of concept-structured residuals.

Some reported results contradict broad claims. For example, on CIFAR10/100 and Camelyon17 with Yeh et al. concepts, CONDA often hurts target performance; on Waterbirds, adapted CBMs remain near the zero-shot baseline and far below source-domain performance. Thus the claim of aligning CBM performance with non-interpretable classification is only partially supported.

Interpretability evaluation lacks rigorous empirical validity. Automatic concept annotation via CLIP/ConceptNet and coherence regularization are used, but there is no human study, no faithfulness metric, and no quantitative comparison showing that residual concepts are semantically meaningful rather than merely predictive directions.
